name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,764

entries.clue: Innocent Bobby binding hand initially cut (4,4)

indicators.note: the policeman binds the letter, holding it inside
take only the first letter of 'hand'

blocks.note: a lamb is the traditional picture of innocence
a bobby is a British policeman, named after Sir Robert Peel

annotation.surface: An innocent policeman ties up a hand whose first bit has been cut.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bobby' looks like a first name, and 'cut' like part of the story, but 'cut' is the definition: the butcher's sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A butcher's cut is a portion of meat, and a lamb chop is one such cut, so this is definition by example in reverse.

entries.clue: Stupid visionary sent up expansionist monarchy (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending a word up writes it from bottom to top

blocks.note: an ass is a stupid person
airy = visionary, full of impractical ideas

annotation.surface: A foolish dreamer is mocked by an empire bent on conquest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' reads as mocked, but here it turns the word for visionary upside down in the down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: Assyria was an ancient Mesopotamian kingdom whose kings conquered their way to a vast empire, which is what 'expansionist monarchy' describes.

entries.clue: Wretched Bradley's initial disclosure of documents (5)

indicators.note: take only the first letter of 'Bradley'

blocks.note: an unauthorised release of documents to the press

annotation.surface: The sorry tale of Bradley Manning and the leaked military documents.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface points to Bradley (now Chelsea) Manning, who leaked US military documents; only the initial is used.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: wretched and bleak both describe a miserable, hopeless state.

entries.clue: Cheer up then crashing down? Not easily achieved (4-3)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' writes the word from bottom to top
a word that crashes breaks apart, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: rah is a cheer, as in hurrah

annotation.surface: Someone cheers, then comes crashing down: a victory that cost a lot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Down' is not a direction here but the four letters that get jumbled.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain paraphrase: what is won only with hard effort was not easily achieved.

entries.clue: Questions politician involved in unpleasant matter (5)

indicators.note: the politician is wrapped up inside the other word

blocks.note: the matter from an infected wound

annotation.surface: A question about a politician mixed up in some nasty business.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Questions' is a verb, not a noun. 'Unpleasant matter' reads as a scandal but is meant literally, the stuff in a wound.
annotation.definitionFit: Pump has the informal sense of questioning someone persistently for information, so it is a verb synonym here.

entries.clue: Trap set by eleven miserable Spanish bankers? (6)

indicators.note: the banks of each word are its two edges, so take the outer letters

annotation.surface: A football team of gloomy Spanish bankers falls into a trap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spanish bankers' looks like people who work in banks in Spain. The question mark flags that 'bankers' means the banks, the edges, of the three words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to enmesh is to catch as if in a mesh or net, which is to trap.

entries.clue: Once-healthy duke blew out (7)

annotation.surface: A duke who used to be fit is now out of breath.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'Once-healthy' glues two pieces of wordplay together for the surface; split it and each word gives its own chunk.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to blow out air is to breathe out.

entries.clue: General answer found in Mark Chapter 9? (9)

indicators.note: the answer's A is found inside the two abbreviations

blocks.note: 9 across is the tennis player Arthur Ashe; this takes his first name

annotation.surface: Looking up a verse in the Gospel of Mark, chapter nine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mark Chapter 9' reads as a Bible reference, but the 9 is a cross-reference to the answer at 9 across, and it is that player's first name that is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Douglas MacArthur was an American general of the Second World War and Korea.

entries.clue: Mistress last month put in clinic close to Chelsea (7)

indicators.note: the month goes inside the clinic
the close of Chelsea is its final letter

blocks.note: ult. = ultimo, 'of last month', in old business letters

annotation.surface: A footballer's mistress booked into a clinic near Chelsea last month.
annotation.walkthrough: ULT is the old commercial abbreviation for ultimo, as in 'your letter of the 5th ult.'
annotation.definitionFit: A less common sense: besides a sultan's wife or mother, a sultana can be a sultan's concubine, a mistress.

entries.clue: Winner at court remains for hearing (4)

indicators.note: the answer is something that sounds like the word for remains

annotation.surface: A winner in a court case whose remains are kept for a hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Court' and 'hearing' suggest a law case, but the court is a tennis court.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Arthur Ashe won the Wimbledon singles in 1975, a winner on court.

entries.clue: Decrepit couple on strike (10)

indicators.note: in an across answer, A on B puts A after B, so couple goes second

blocks.note: to ram is to strike hard
to couple, join with a chain

annotation.surface: A worn-out old couple walk out on strike.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Couple' reads as two people, but here it is a verb, to join with a chain.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a ramshackle building is falling apart, decrepit.

entries.clue: City craft back carrying Russian rifle (6)

indicators.note: the word for craft is written backwards
the reversed word carries the rifle inside it

annotation.surface: A boat returns to a city with a Russian gun on board.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Craft' suggests a boat, but it is skilled work.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Krakow is a large historic city in southern Poland.

entries.clue: Dark soil disturbed in trade route (4,4)

indicators.note: the letters are disturbed, put out of order

annotation.surface: Dark earth churned up along an old trading path.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a road being dug up, which fits the answer's picture while hiding that 'disturbed' works on the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Silk Road was the ancient network of routes carrying trade between China and the West.

entries.clue: Closely connected, return bananas? (4,2,4)

blocks.note: to return homework is to submit it
the name for a bunch of bananas

annotation.surface: An odd query about whether some bananas are being sent back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' could mean mad, but the greengrocer's term for a cluster of them is what is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: two things that go hand in hand are closely linked, like people holding hands.

entries.clue: Oscar having way with incredibly dry wit that may offend (5,4)

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer, 'something that may offend', rather than being a noun itself

indicators.note: the letters are arranged in an unbelievable way

blocks.note: O is Oscar in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Oscar Wilde, famous for his wit, finds his dry humour gives offence.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface summons Oscar Wilde, but Oscar only gives a single letter; the jumbled dry wit comes first in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a dirty word is a rude or taboo word, the kind that may offend.

entries.clue: Greatest length trunk road spans? (3)

indicators.note: the road stretches across the length, holding it inside

blocks.note: the A1, Britain's longest trunk road, with the 1 read as I

annotation.surface: Which trunk road covers the greatest distance?
annotation.walkthrough: The A1 is the main road from London to Edinburgh; the digit 1 is treated as the letter I.
annotation.definitionFit: A nickname: the boxer Muhammad Ali called himself The Greatest, and the name stuck.

entries.clue: Gull in trees with aspiration called out (4)

indicators.note: the answer is what the trees with an H sound like when spoken

blocks.note: aspiration is an H sound breathed before OAKS

annotation.surface: A seagull up in the trees, breathing hard and calling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gull' is a verb meaning to fool, not the bird. Aspiration is the H breathed before a vowel.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to gull someone is to dupe them, which is what a hoax does.

entries.clue: Irish drawn to Patrick, say, excited reaction? (4)

blocks.note: Patrick is an example of a saint, abbreviated ST

annotation.surface: The Irish flock to St Patrick's Day celebrations with a buzz.
annotation.walkthrough: The Irish letters are drawn to, placed beside, the saint, so the saint comes first.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun sense: a stir is a flurry of excitement or commotion in response to something.

entries.clue: Three card players in silly female attire (7)

indicators.note: the card players go in the silly person

blocks.note: a silly person, as in 'you silly!'
North, South, East: three of the four players at bridge

annotation.surface: Three bridge players turn up in ridiculous women's clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: Bridge players are named for the compass points, so any three of the four letters N, E, S, W can appear.
annotation.definitionFit: A British garment: a twinset is a matching jumper and cardigan traditionally worn by women.

entries.clue: Crew crossing one watercourse displays standard (10)

indicators.note: the crew stretches across the one, holding it inside

blocks.note: to man a ship is to crew it

annotation.surface: A rowing crew crossing a river shows off its flag.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crew' is a verb here; 'standard' is an adjective meaning usual, not a flag.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective synonym: mainstream ideas are the conventional, standard ones.

entries.clue: Sage Derby perhaps eaten by mum twice (7)

indicators.note: the hat goes inside the two mums

blocks.note: a derby is a bowler hat

annotation.surface: A cheese, Sage Derby, gobbled up by mum not once but twice.
annotation.walkthrough: Sage Derby is an English cheese flavoured with sage, so the surface is about eating; but 'Sage' is the definition and the derby is headgear.
annotation.definitionFit: A title as synonym: in India a mahatma is a revered great soul, a sage, as in Mahatma Gandhi.

entries.clue: One looking small — ceramics worker? (7)

annotation.surface: A potter who looks a bit small.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One looking small' reads as someone who appears little; the definition ends at 'looking'.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a spotter is someone who watches out, as a trainspotter or aircraft spotter does.

entries.clue: Tough resistance shown by pair coming in down under? (7)

indicators.note: the resistance and the pair come inside the country

annotation.surface: A pair of tough immigrants arrive in Australia.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Down under' is lower case, so it reads as a direction, but it is the nickname for Australia.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an arduous task is tough, demanding great effort.

entries.clue: The legendary king of rock-and-roll (8)

blocks.note: a king from myth, not the pop sense of 'legend'
read literally: one who rolls a rock

annotation.surface: A tribute to Elvis Presley, the legendary King of Rock and Roll.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase is Elvis Presley's title, but read literally it is a mythical king who rolls a rock, punished forever to push a boulder uphill.
annotation.definitionFit: In Greek myth King Sisyphus of Corinth is condemned to roll a rock up a hill for eternity, a literal king of rock-rolling.

entries.clue: Period charm (5)

blocks.note: a stretch of time, as in a dry one

annotation.walkthrough: Two unrelated meanings of one word sit side by side; 'Period charm' reads as the appeal of an old costume drama.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: a spell of weather is a period, and a witch's spell is a charm.

entries.clue: Vicious perhaps to stop one being supportive (6)

indicators.note: the name plugs the middle of the word, stopping it like a cork

blocks.note: Sid Vicious, bass player of the Sex Pistols

annotation.surface: A cruel person tries to stop someone from being helpful.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vicious' looks like an adjective, but the capital and 'perhaps' mark a punk rocker's stage surname, from which his first name is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: to be onside is to be on someone's side, backing them.

entries.clue: Gloomy bachelor in northern town (5)

indicators.note: the bachelor goes in the town

blocks.note: Sale is a town near Manchester in northern England

annotation.surface: A miserable single man living in a northern town.
annotation.walkthrough: The town reads as a shop event, but Sale is a town in Greater Manchester.
annotation.definitionFit: A poetic sense: sable, the heraldic black, is used to mean dark and gloomy.

entries.clue: Mattress on ground and many different things (10)

indicators.note: the letters are ground up and reformed

annotation.surface: A mattress lying on the ground surrounded by a clutter of odds and ends.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On ground' reads as lying on the floor, but 'on' is fodder and 'ground' means crushed.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a mixed collection is made up of many different things.

entries.clue: Stench from pit all right in Ulysses? (4)

blocks.note: BO = body odour, the smell from an armpit

annotation.surface: A bad smell from a pit is fine in James Joyce's novel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pit' suggests a mine, but it is the armpit. The question mark flags Ulysses as just one example.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Joyce's Ulysses is one instance of the general category the answer names.

entries.clue: Venues constructed in stone with return of opera (6)

indicators.note: the opera is written going back, right to left

blocks.note: st = stone, the British weight of 14 pounds

annotation.surface: Stone-built arenas that see the return of an opera.
annotation.walkthrough: The stone is the British unit of weight, not building stone.
annotation.definitionFit: A Latin plural: stadiums are sports venues, and stadia is their classical plural.

entries.clue: Big ship linked with Spain's generosity (8)

blocks.note: E = Spain, its international vehicle code

annotation.surface: A huge Spanish ship loaded with lavish gifts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spain's' is a possessive for the surface; the wordplay uses only the country's code.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from French: largesse is open-handed giving, generosity.
